title.narrative: Scaling catalytic solutions for climate-resilient food systems in Africa

description.narrative: The expected outputs of the project are to 1) involve 100 decision makers, organize at least 10 stakeholder meetings, publish 5 publications identifying lock-ins per country, and publishing 6 publications documenting the process of deal borkering, and 3) involve 20 partners through the activities, linking to 6 ongoing policy processes

The objectives of the project are to 1) reach 6 deals and pilots (1 deal per country) on game-changing food systems innovations that unlock a current lock-in, 2) Redirect/inform USD 20M that are focused on food systems transformation, and 3) reach 300,000 farmers and 20MSMEs through deals and investments

The project seeks to enhance the climate-resilience of African food systems through evidence generation, stakeholder engagement and outreach, that helps scale catalytic solutions in six Eastern and Southern African countries (Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, Rwanda, Zambia and Zimbabwe).

recipient-country.narrative: Clim-Eat aims to support the Government of Tanzania in repurposing its agricultural input subsidies to incentivize sustainable soil health practices. The Tanzanian government provides subsidies on agricultural inputs like fertilizers and seeds through the National Agricultural Input Voucher Scheme (NAIVS) program currently reaching 5 million farmers. The subsidy aims to make inputs more affordable and accessible to smallholder farmers, leading to increased adoption of improved inputs and higher crop yields. The system is based on e-vouchers, often distributed through mobile technology. The Government of Tanzania is implementing a pilot program targeting 15,000 farmers, focusing on reducing soil acidity in the Southern Highlands by incentivizing integrated soil fertility management practices. Soil testing is a key component of the pilot program for which the government is applying mobile soil testing facilities, an innovative approach in the region. The advised soil management practices are informed by outcomes of soil testing throughout, resulting in tailored advice to farmers included in the pilot.

Clim-Eat is working on the topic of repurposing agricultural input subsidies in Zambia, similar to Tanzania and Malawi. The Zambian repurposing model, however, entails innovative features that could serve as inspiration for other countries in the region. Zambia’s Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) reaches 1 million farmers and is fully digitally integrated with other relevant digital databases which facilitates easier monitoring of subsidized farmers. Thereby, the Government of Zambia integrates digital market connections for subsidizes farmers, improving market access for farmers. The Government of Zambia aims to add soil testing to the FISP and therefore knowledge exchange with the Government of Tanzania could be beneficial.

In 2026, Clim-Eat aims to operate in Zimbabwe. There are three areas of work, each with a different impact pathway. In all three areas, there will be assessments of the carbon mitigation potential of the technologies, and complementary work on carbon finance and options for the Voluntary Carbon Market (VCM): A. Expanding solar irrigation for the cultivation of indigenous vegetables. This is important as it reduces the dependence on rainfed agriculture and is regarded as a key adaptation option. Africa is extremely under-irrigated despite enormous potential for expansion and is also energy-poor. Indigenous vegetables are rich in nutrients and demand is increasing from urban dwellers. The energy and agricultural ministries have had limited interaction, so a key lever for change is fostering that link, so that agro-voltaic solutions become mainstreamed in development – for both energy provision and food security, for climate adaptation and mitigation. Work will include perfecting the technology as well as fostering production-consumption linkages. B. Diversifying farmer income from non-timber forest products. Here the focus is on the Tamarindus tree and the products that can be derived from it. These trees grow in semi-arid areas where farming is extremely difficult. As an adaptation option the plan is to expand Tamarindus production, so that farmers can derive income from a more reliable source. A Tamarindus processing plant is being set up. Work will involve identifying suitable expansion areas (in the face of climate change), empowering producer groups, and marketing products to stimulate demand. Currently a Zambian Tamarindus product dominates the Zimbabwean market. C. Conservation agriculture is important for both climate change adaptation and mitigation, but positive outcomes from the practices are very context specific (e.g. dependent on soil type, farmer assets etc.). The government has a program – Pfumvudza – that provides inputs to farmers conditional on their practicing conservation agriculture. This covers 200.000 ha. The program is one-size-fits-all so does not consider context. The program is due to be phased out and replaced by a new program, so this represents a possible opportunity for impact. The work will involve assessing different conservation agricultural practices and convening stakeholders to come up with new options that consider context.

In Kenya, Clim-Eat collaborates with partners to incentivize the uptake of agricultural insurance among small-scale farmers. In Kenya, approximately 2% of farmers and pastoralists are covered by agricultural insurance, leading to financial vulnerability across the sector. Main reasons for the low uptake of agricultural insurance are overall low awareness of the availability of agricultural insurance, limited accessibility to the product, low trust in insurance providers and high premiums. The pilot aims to address these lock-ins by scaling up awareness creation among farmers of the product by training ‘champion farmers’, who subsequently train farmers in their communities (train-the-trainer approach). These champion farmers often hold trusted positions within their communities and therewith support in creating trust around the product. ACRE Africa developed a mobile app (DigiBima) in which farmers can self-register their farm, relevant agricultural data, pay for premiums, and at the end of the season (when eligible) receive the insurance cover in their digital wallet (MPesa). Kenyan farmers are naturally weary of new tools, especially when they need to pay for. One of the most important aspects of scaling insurance is that payouts need to happen as soon as possible after season closing to ensure that farmer trust is not lost. Finally, to incentivize the uptake of agricultural insurance, the pilot provides a 40% subsidy to farmers to lower the threshold of trialing the product. The aim is to lower the subsidy over time, or to convince the government to provide subsidies to create sustainability of the pilot’s efforts.

In Malawi, Clim-Eat is informing a pilot by the National Government, the World Bank, and other implementation partners, to repurpose agricultural input subsidies to incentivize 24,000 farmers (out of a total of 36,000 farmers) to shift to better soil health management practices that enhance adaptation and livelihood security. In the African continent overall, the extent of soil degradation is alarming. About 63-65% of the continent's cultivated land is reportedly degraded. This degradation affects over 485 million people (65% of the population), and projections suggest that more than half of Africa's arable land may become unusable by 2050. Soil degradation has negative implications for both climate change adaptation and mitigation. The Eastern and Southern African region (including Malawi, Tanzania, Kenya and Zambia) is considered among the regions in Africa that are heavily affected by soil degradation. Malawi's food system is facing a crisis. With over 29 tons of topsoil lost per hectare annually, the country's soil degradation rate is ten times the global average. This threatens food production, farmer livelihoods, and long-term sustainability. To address this challenge, the pilot provides soil health packages and financial incentives, trying to identify mechanisms to reward farmers for adopting sustainable soil health practices. Malawi is one of the frontrunners considering the repurposing of agricultural input subsidies and serves as example for many countries in the region. The pilot is running until 2027 and will inform policy development on agricultural subsidies. If successful, it is anticipated to impact 1 million Malawian farmers. In Malawi, the most interesting addition to the repurposing program is an organo-mineral fertilizer, locally called Mbeya. Replacing traditional (imported) inorganic fertilizer with Mbeya could significantly reduce costs of the governmental subsidy program whilst simultaneously contributing to soil health, food security and adaptation and mitigation.

In Rwanda, Clim-Eat is collaborating with partners to scale up the application of Digital Climate Advisory Services (DCAS) to increase maize and soybean yields. Rolling out DCAS can significantly contribute to scaling up the number of farmers that can be reached with relevant climate advisories, especially in countries like Rwanda where most extension services are still provided in person (which severely limits the number of farmers can that be reached in a short timeframe). Currently, a pilot is implemented, reaching 2,500 farmers in the country. If proven successful, the pilot can be scaled to 60,000-90,000 farmers.
